layers.name: Knowledge Compilation
layers.description: Transforming heterogeneous human knowledge into structured, navigable semantic artifacts — organized before the question is asked.
layers.problem: Human knowledge is scattered across documents, notes, and code. Until it is compiled into navigable structure, it cannot be understood at scale.
layers.why_matters: Compilation is the first step in reducing the cost of understanding: it turns a corpus into something a person can actually explore.

layers.name: Compile-Time AI
layers.description: Performing reasoning once and compiling it into representations people can explore, instead of rediscovering relationships on every query. An active, recent direction of the research.
layers.problem: Query-time AI rediscovers the same relationships repeatedly. Reasoning done ahead of time is far cheaper to reuse.
layers.why_matters: Compile-time AI is how we lower the cognitive cost of understanding — the hard work happens once, for everyone.

layers.name: Scientific Knowledge Systems
layers.description: Semantic infrastructure for preserving scientific knowledge and accelerating discovery — making research easier to build upon.
layers.problem: Scientific knowledge is fragmented across papers, code, and institutions. Preserving and connecting it accelerates everyone who comes next.
layers.why_matters: Every hour a researcher spends searching is an hour not spent discovering. Better knowledge systems return that time to science.

layers.name: Local-First AI
layers.description: Knowledge systems that run on your own hardware — transparent, inspectable, and under the user’s control rather than a third party’s cloud.
layers.problem: Cloud-dependent AI places knowledge behind someone else’s infrastructure and incentives. Local-first keeps it under the user’s control.
layers.why_matters: Knowledge that can be shared without being consumed should also be owned. Local-first is how understanding stays sovereign.

layers.name: Cognitive Memory
layers.description: Persistent, structured memory that compounds understanding across sessions instead of forgetting it between conversations.
layers.problem: Systems that forget between sessions cannot accumulate understanding. Memory is what turns information into knowledge.
layers.why_matters: Durable memory is how the cost of understanding keeps falling — each session builds on the last instead of starting over.

layers.name: Research Automation
layers.description: Autonomous and semi-autonomous agents that ingest, synthesize, and broadcast knowledge — returning time to human discovery and care.
layers.problem: Much knowledge work is ingestion, synthesis, and reporting. Automating it returns human time to judgment and care.
layers.why_matters: Automation at the level of understanding — not replacement — is how more people can do more meaningful work.

layers.name: Knowledge Representation
layers.description: How understanding is modeled and made explicit — from intermediate representations to structured publishing of what we know.
layers.problem: Understanding that cannot be represented cannot be reused, taught, or improved. Representation is the substrate of transfer.
layers.why_matters: Clear representation is what makes knowledge portable — from one mind to another, from one system to the next.

layers.name: Decision Graphs
layers.description: Explicit representations of judgment that make reasoning inspectable, reusable, and improvable over time.
layers.problem: Judgment is usually implicit and unrepeatable. Making it explicit lets reasoning be inspected and taught.
layers.why_matters: When decisions are graphs, not black boxes, understanding becomes something we can pass on and refine.

title: Research Directions
subtitle: One mission. Eight directions. Forty-plus experiments toward reducing the cost of understanding human knowledge.
narrative: None of these projects is the destination. Each is a different approach toward the same goal — making human knowledge cheaper to understand, preserve, and share.
